chapters.title: Chapter 2: Framing Trading as a Machine Learning Problem

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Target: Returns, Direction, or Volatility?

children.text: Three prop trading applicants sit down with the exact same five years of Nifty data. One builds a model to predict tomorrow's direction. Another builds a model to predict tomorrow's return, the actual size and sign of the move. The third builds a model to predict how much the Nifty will move over the next week, regardless of direction. All three are doing 'machine learning for trading' on the same underlying data. None of them are solving the same problem, and none of their models would even be useful for the other two applicants' goals. Lesson 5 showed that the label matters more than the model. This lesson is about the biggest label decision of all: what kind of question are you actually asking?

body.text: Direction, return magnitude, and volatility are three genuinely different targets, not three flavors of the same problem. Each supports a different kind of trading decision, entry signals, conviction sizing, or risk sizing, and choosing the wrong one for your actual goal produces a model that can be statistically sound and still useless.

children.text: Direction: Will It Go Up or Down?

A direction target, the classification approach from Lesson 5, asks the simplest possible question: up or down, using a deadband to drop ambiguous, tiny moves. Its appeal is that it maps directly onto a simple decision, go long or go short. Its weakness is exactly what Lesson 4's case study demonstrated: direction alone says nothing about how large a move is likely to be, so a model can be highly accurate at calling direction and still lose money if it has no sense of how much conviction, or how much risk, sits behind each call.
Return Magnitude: How Much Will It Move, and Which Way?

A return magnitude target uses regression instead of classification: predict the actual forward return, a number, not a bucket. This carries more information than direction alone, a model that expects a small up move and one that expects a large up move can now be sized differently, rather than treated identically. The honest catch is that returns are dominated by noise, and published quant research routinely reports out-of-sample R-squared values in the low single digits for return prediction models, meaning the model explains only a small slice of what actually happens. This is not a failure. A model that genuinely, consistently explains even 2 to 3 percent of out-of-sample return variance, if that edge survives Lesson 2's signal and execution layers, can be a real, tradeable result. The mistake beginners make is expecting an R-squared anywhere close to what a model gets on a typical non-financial regression problem, and concluding the whole approach is broken when it inevitably does not show up.

body.label: Typical out-of-sample R-squared for a genuinely useful return model
body.value: often in the low single digits
body.context: Financial returns are overwhelmingly noise. A model that reliably explains even 2 to 3 percent of return variance out of sample can represent a real, tradeable edge, not a failed model.

children.text: Volatility: How Much Will It Move, Regardless of Direction?

markDefs.definition: A backward-looking measure of how much a security has actually moved over a given historical window, typically calculated as the standard deviation of its returns, often annualized.

children.text: A volatility target asks a third, completely different question: not which way will price move, but how much will it move, in either direction.

, the rolling standard deviation of returns, is the standard building block, and it is worth noticing that this is the exact same calculation Lesson 6 used as a feature. What has changed is not the formula, it is the question. As a feature, it describes recent turbulence, known information as of today. As a target in this lesson, it becomes something you are trying to forecast for a future window, useful for position sizing and risk controls in Chapter 4, and for options strategy decisions, since a trader can profit from volatility itself, through instruments like a straddle, without taking any view on direction at all.

body.caption: The same calculation, used as a feature versus used as a target
body.code:
import numpy as np

# As a FEATURE (Lesson 6): describes recent turbulence, known as of today
df["realized_vol_20d"] = df["ret_1d"].rolling(20).std() * np.sqrt(252)

# As a LABEL for a volatility-target problem: shift it forward, so today's
# features are used to predict the NEXT window's volatility, not describe today's
df["target_vol_20d_fwd"] = df["ret_1d"].rolling(20).std().shift(-20) * np.sqrt(252)

body.caption: Three target types, side by side

cells: Will price move up or down
Ignores magnitude entirely; can pass the Lesson 4 accuracy trap
How much, and which way, will price move
Genuinely low R-squared is normal; needs care to separate real edge from noise
How much will price move, regardless of direction
Mean squared error on realized volatility
Says nothing about direction; cannot generate a buy or sell signal on its own

body.text: A trader who expects the Nifty to move sharply on Union Budget day or an RBI policy day, but has no real conviction about direction, is exactly the case where a volatility target is more useful than a directional one. The relevant decision is whether to buy a straddle or strangle at all, and how to size it, not which single direction to bet on.

body.title: Matching the target to the goal
body.question: A prop trading applicant wants to build a model that decides how large a position to take on each trade, scaling size down during turbulent periods, regardless of whether the market is expected to go up or down. Which target should this model predict?
options: None of these, position sizing cannot use machine learning
body.explanation: The stated goal is purely about how much the market is likely to move, not which way, which is exactly what a volatility target answers. Direction is irrelevant to this specific decision, and return magnitude bundles in a directional component the trader explicitly does not need here.

body.title: Choosing a target for a Budget-day options strategy
body.scenario: A trader believes the Nifty will move sharply on Union Budget day but has no strong view on whether it will rise or fall. She is considering buying a Nifty straddle, a long call and a long put at the same strike, and wants a model to help decide how large a position to take.
body.prompt: Which target, direction, return magnitude, or volatility, is most relevant to this decision, and would a directional model even help here at all?
body.modelAnswer: Volatility is the relevant target. A straddle profits from a large move in either direction and loses money mainly if the market stays unusually calm, so the decision that actually matters is how large a move to expect, not which way it goes. A directional model would not help meaningfully here, and could even be actively misleading: it might indicate a mild view on direction while telling the trader nothing about whether the move will be large enough to justify the premium paid for the straddle, which is precisely the question a volatility target is built to answer.

cards.definition: A classification label describing whether price is expected to move up or down, typically with a deadband to drop ambiguous, tiny moves.
A regression label describing the actual forward return, capturing both size and direction of an expected move.
A regression label describing how much a security is expected to move, in either direction, over a future window.
A backward-looking measure of how much a security has actually moved over a given historical window, typically calculated as the standard deviation of its returns, often annualized.
A measure of how much of a target's variance a model explains. In financial return prediction, values in the low single digits are common and can still represent a real, tradeable edge.

points: Direction, return magnitude, and volatility are three genuinely different targets, each suited to a different kind of trading decision.
A direction target supports a simple entry signal but ignores magnitude entirely, the exact gap that caused Lesson 4's accuracy paradox.
A return magnitude target carries more information but comes with genuinely low out-of-sample R-squared as the normal, expected outcome, not a sign of failure.

A volatility target answers a completely different question, how much will price move, regardless of direction, useful for position sizing and for options strategies like straddles that profit from movement itself.
The exact same calculation, such as rolling standard deviation of returns, can serve as a feature in one problem and a label in another. What changes is the question you are asking, not the formula.
